newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends up as modest recovery continues.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends up as modest recovery continues.

text.p: COMEX copper ended firmer Friday, the market partly recovered from its steep selloff in the past week, but there was still much damage to be repaired, dealers said.
"The overall uptrend remains intact," analyst John Gross of the Copper Journal said. "It will take a few days for the market to regain its composure. The fundamentals have not changed."
Most-active September COMEX settled 0.95 cent firmer at 111.85 cents a lb. Spot July went out 1.05 cent higher at 113.00 cents.
September copper is still 4.25 cents down on the week.

The market is largely focused on the LME July options expiry next Wednesday, and delta hedging - the need to buy or sell futures to cover options positions as prices rise or fall - will continue to fuel volatility up to that time, dealers said.
LME cash to three months backwardation remained firm at $145/$155.
LME stocks are still low despite increases this week, but merchants noted the market at this time of year traditionally enters a seasonal slowdown in the North West hemisphere.
LME stocks rose 150 tonnes Friday to 124,900 tonnes. Some metal was expected to flow from COMEX to LME on the back of arbitrage deals when July LME was at a good premium over July COMEX.
COMEX stocks totalled 48,565 short tons Thursday.

The strike at Inco Ltd's Sudbury mining operations since June 2 may be resolved this weekend when workers vote for the second time on a new pay deal. Apart from being a major nickel producer, the company also supplies copper to the Northeastern U.S.

Open interest in COMEX copper has fell sharply as the heavy selloff spilled over into the early part of the week. At close of trade Thursday, there were 49,096 lots of open interest, down from a peak of about 60,000 mid-May.

Gross said it was constructive that open interest fell along with prices. "The two together suggest higher prices. You can infer that, to some degree, the selling was longs getting out of the market rather than shorts coming in," he added.
Much of the week's selling by speculators, who had been overwhelmingly long on COMEX, dealers said.
